cards.headline: Two people, one trade, two outcomes.
cards.body: Same stock, same entry, same exit. One puts 2% of the account at risk, the other puts 40%. The idea was identical. Only the size was different, and only one of them still has an account to trade with.

cards.headline: Size is a loss decision.
cards.body: Most people size a position by how much they want to make. The question that actually sets the number is the opposite one: how much are you prepared to lose if this goes wrong? Answer that first and the share count falls out of it.

cards.headline: Three numbers, one formula.
cards.body: Pick a maximum loss per trade as a fraction of the account. That is your risk budget, in dollars. Divide it by the distance from your entry price to your exit price. **Shares = (account x risk fraction) / (entry - exit).**

cards.headline: Run it once with round numbers.
cards.body: A 10,000 account. Cap the loss on one trade at 1%, so 100 is the risk budget. Entry at 50, exit at 45, so each share can lose 5. 100 divided by 5 is **20 shares**. That is 1,000 of stock — a tenth of the account.

cards.prompt: Same account, same 100 risk budget, same entry at 50. You move the exit down from 45 to 40. What happens to the share count?
cards.explanation: Per-share risk doubled from 5 to 10, so the size has to halve: 100 divided by 10 is **10 shares**. A wider exit does not buy you room. It buys you fewer shares.

cards.title: Wider exit, smaller position
cards.caption: Entry stays at 50 and the risk budget stays at 100. As the exit moves further away, per-share risk grows and the position collapses. Every bar risks the same 100.

cards.body: Your risk budget in dollars, divided by the [[1]] risk, gives you the number of shares.
cards.explanation: Dollars at risk, divided by dollars at risk per share, equals shares. Notice what the formula never asks about: the price you hope to sell at.

cards.headline: The fraction is a dial, not a law.
cards.body: Roughly one to two percent per trade is what most risk-management texts describe. It is a convention, and it is yours to set — nobody else can set it for you. Halve the fraction and every position halves with it. The arithmetic is fixed. The input is personal.

cards.title: Turning the dial
cards.caption: Same 10,000 account, entry at 50, exit at 45. Only the risk fraction moves. Shares track it in a straight line: double the fraction, double the position.

cards.body: Only three inputs move the share count. Change one and the size changes with it. Nothing else about the trade enters the arithmetic.

cards.summary: Position size is arithmetic, not ambition. Decide the loss you can carry, then let the share count follow.
bullets: A wider exit always means fewer shares, never more.
The risk fraction is a dial you set yourself, not a rule handed to you.

cards.insight: Size a position by what it can cost you, never by what you hope it pays. The arithmetic only runs in one direction.
